issues.description: Attribute 'age' on class Animal: The UML in the problem statement declares Animal with attributes 'name: String' (problem_statement.md lines 27) and 'age: int' (problem_statement.md line 28). The solution implementation (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Animal.java) defines only a private field 'name' and does not declare an 'age' attribute. This mismatch leaves students unclear whether they must implement and initialize an 'age' field on Animal, or omit it.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the attribute design consistent across artifacts. Either (A) remove the 'age: int' attribute from the UML and any textual descriptions so Animal has only 'name' (update problem_statement.md and the UML), or (B) add a private int age field to Animal in the template and solution, update the Animal constructor to accept and initialize age, and update any examples/text to mention age. Ensure the template, UML, problem text, and solution all reflect the same set of attributes.

issues.description: Constructor parameters for class Animal: The UML in the problem statement specifies a constructor signature Animal(String, int) (name and age) (problem_statement.md line 29). The solution's Animal constructor signature is Animal(String) (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Animal.java line 6). This inconsistency leaves students uncertain whether to implement a one-parameter constructor (name only) or a two-parameter constructor (name and age), and whether to store an age field.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the constructor signature across all artifacts. Either (A) update the UML and problem text to require Animal(String) and remove age from the constructor and attributes, or (B) update the template and solution to provide Animal(String, int), add an 'age' field, and initialize it. Ensure examples and tests (if any) use the chosen constructor consistently.

issues.description: The concept is the Animal class's attributes and constructor signature. In the problem statement UML (lines show an abstract Animal with attributes name: String and age: int and a constructor Animal(String, int)), the Animal is specified to have two attributes (name and age) and a constructor taking (String, int). In the template and solution code, the implemented Animal class only declares a single attribute 'name' and defines a constructor Animal(String) (Solution: src/de/tum/cit/ase/Animal.java constructor at line 6). This mismatch (problem statement expects Animal(String, int) and an 'age' field; code expects Animal(String) and no 'age') creates confusion for students about which constructor and attributes to implement, how subclasses should call super(...), and whether example usages in Main should pass one or two arguments. Students following the UML could implement different constructors/fields than the provided template/solution and encounter compilation/test mismatches.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the Animal specification consistent across artifacts. Either: (A) Update the problem statement/UML to remove the 'age' attribute and change the UML constructor to Animal(String), documenting that Animal has only a name; update the UML lines and any textual references so they match the code and sample usages (Main). Or: (B) Update the template and solution code to include an 'age' int field and change constructors to Animal(String, int), updating all subclass constructors (Seal, Pig, Goat) to accept and pass the age to super(name, age), and update sample usages in Main and any test fixtures to supply the age argument. Choose one option and apply it to all files (problem_statement.md, template Farm/Main, solution Animal/Seal/Pig/Goat and their usages) so students have a single, unambiguous specification to implement.
